title: India's Tech Hubs Are No Longer Back Offices. They're Filing 90,000 Patents a Year.
excerpt: At a Reuters summit in Bengaluru, executives from Daimler Truck, Kimberly-Clark, and Publicis said AI is turning India's global capability centres from cost-saving outposts into innovation engines — but a patent office with fewer than 1,000 examiners is the bottleneck.
body:
For two decades, the story of India's global capability centres was a simple one: skilled talent at scale, at low cost. American and European multinationals opened offices in Bengaluru, Hyderabad, and Pune to handle back-office operations, customer support, and routine software tasks. The value proposition was labor arbitrage — the same work, done by qualified engineers, for a fraction of the price.

That story is over.

At a Reuters summit in Bengaluru this week, executives from Daimler Truck, Kimberly-Clark, Publicis Groupe's Epsilon, and other global firms described a transformation that has been building quietly for years and is now accelerating under the force of artificial intelligence: India's GCCs are becoming the places where intellectual property is created, not just where instructions are followed.

## The Numbers

India now houses more than 2,100 global capability centres employing 2.36 million people and generating nearly $100 billion in annual revenue — a milestone the industry hit four years ahead of schedule, according to a 2026 Nasscom-Zinnov report.

Patent filings in India rose 11.3 percent to over 90,000 in fiscal 2024, with nearly half filed by multinational companies. And executives say even that number understates India's contribution — because much of the intellectual property generated in Indian centres is filed through parent entities in the United States and Europe, where the process is faster.

"The number of IPs, the patents and the trade secrets created by GCCs in India is already increasing," said Radhakrishnan Kodakkal, head of Daimler Truck Innovation Center India, at the summit. "AI would accelerate it."

## From Cost Centre to Innovation Engine

The shift is visible across industries. Kimberly-Clark, the consumer goods giant behind Huggies and Kleenex, has used an India-built AI platform to cut content creation time from nearly a month to two hours. The platform also identifies influencers and localizes campaigns across markets.

"Content creation two years back took 24 days but now it only takes two hours due to AI," said Deena Dayalan, Kimberly-Clark's global head of digital operations and cloud transformation.

At Epsilon, Publicis Groupe's data-driven marketing arm, managing director Pratik Nath said he expects "more and more IP work" to originate from India. Novo Nordisk, the Danish pharmaceutical giant, is using AI to accelerate drug launches while expanding India's role in global operations. Daimler Truck's Indian engineers are using AI tools to "generate IP faster."

The common thread: AI is not replacing these workers. It is promoting them — elevating Indian teams from execution to invention.

## The Bottleneck No One Talks About

But India's patent infrastructure has not kept pace with the innovation it is producing.

Filing a patent in India can take five to six months — roughly double the time in the United States, according to Dayalan. The Indian Patent Office has fewer than 1,000 examiners, compared to more than 8,000 at the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office. Unlike the American system, which begins examining applications automatically upon filing, India requires a separate request to begin substantive review — an extra bureaucratic step that compounds the backlog.

"At the Indian Patent Office, backlog and manpower shortages have long slowed the pace of examination and grant," said Harsh Kaushik, a New Delhi-based intellectual property lawyer.

This is why Kimberly-Clark, despite generating significant intellectual property in India, files all its patents through the United States. It is a quiet admission that India's innovation capacity has outrun its institutional infrastructure.

Recent reforms have helped. The Patent Office has moved more functions online, centralized application allocation, and expanded video hearings. But the gap between what Indian centres are producing and what the Indian patent system can process remains wide.

## The Hiring Paradox

The transformation is also reshaping what GCCs look for in employees. Global firms are rethinking their Indian hiring strategies as AI shifts skill demands. The emphasis is moving from volume to specialization — "niche talents" in AI, cybersecurity, and digital technologies, as Daimler Truck's Kodakkal described it.

Microsoft India president Puneet Chandok told the summit that the GCC workforce is India's greatest strength, but the model needs to evolve from cost arbitrage to capability building. Novo Nordisk plans to expand India's role but will be "conservative" in hiring — a signal that AI-augmented productivity means more output from fewer people.

## What This Means for the Diaspora

For NRIs working in the global tech ecosystem, the GCC transformation is a double-edged development. On one hand, it validates the Indian engineering talent that the diaspora has long championed. On the other, it raises a question many in Silicon Valley have been whispering about: if India's domestic centres can handle core innovation work, what happens to the offshoring-to-onshoring pipeline that has sustained H-1B demand for two decades?

The answer, for now, is that demand is growing at both ends. But the nature of the work is converging. The Indian GCC engineer filing a patent through a U.S. parent company and the Indian-American engineer filing one directly in the U.S. are increasingly doing the same work, in the same domains, on the same products.

The cost advantage has not disappeared. But it is no longer the reason these centres exist.
